value.body: A food technologist develops new food products and improves existing ones and the processes that make them. Packaged-food, beverage, dairy, bakery and ingredient companies hire them. A day involves formulation trials, sensory and shelf-life tests, checking regulatory limits and supporting trials on the plant line.

items.label: Typical entry
items.value: B.Tech / B.Sc Food Technology; M.Tech or M.Sc for R&D posts

items.label: Rules you work with
items.value: FSSAI food standards and labelling regulations

items.label: UG students in Food Technology
items.note: Engineering-stream (B.Tech-level) count; B.Sc programmes may be reported elsewhere. Counts only institutions that responded to AISHE, so national totals may be higher.

items.label: PG students in Food Technology
items.note: ~1,465 under engineering plus ~1,223 under home science; all years. Counts only institutions that responded to AISHE, so national totals may be higher.

value.title: How you get in
value.body: Freshers often start in quality or production at a food plant and move into product development, or join an R&D team directly as a trainee through campus placement or direct application. R&D teams often prefer a master's degree.

value.title: Skills you'll use
items: Reading FSSAI standards and labelling rules

value.title: At a glance
items: Common next roles: senior product developer, R&D manager, regulatory specialist.
Plant experience helps, since new products must run on real production lines.
Product development teams are smaller than quality and production teams.
